title: Revenue recognition
lesson: IFRS 15 requires revenue to be recognised using a 5-step model: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it to the obligations, and recognise revenue as/when each obligation is satisfied - over time if one of the over-time criteria (§35) is met, otherwise at a point in time. Swiss GAAP FER has no equivalent standalone revenue standard; practice instead follows the general prudence/realisation principle in FER 2.
source: IFRS 15 (5-step model, §35 over-time criteria); Swiss GAAP FER 2

title: Non-current assets held for sale
lesson: IFRS 5 requires a non-current asset or disposal group to be classified as 'held for sale' when it is available for immediate sale, the sale is highly probable within one year, and the entity is actively marketing it (§§6-8). Once classified, depreciation stops and the asset is measured at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell. Swiss GAAP FER has no equivalent reclassification standard.

title: Inventories
lesson: IAS 2 requires inventories to be measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value (§9) - cost includes purchase and conversion costs, and NRV is the estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell. Swiss GAAP FER 17 applies the same conservative lower-of logic under the general prudence principle in FER 2.

title: Leases
lesson: IFRS 16 requires lessees to recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the commencement date for virtually all leases (§22), with narrow exemptions for short-term and low-value leases (§§5-8). Swiss GAAP FER 13 still uses the old dual model, distinguishing finance leases (on balance sheet) from operating leases (off balance sheet, disclosed in the notes) - one of the most-tested IFRS-vs-FER differences.

title: Intangible assets
lesson: IAS 38 amortises intangible assets over their useful life, except those with an indefinite useful life, which are instead tested for impairment at least annually under IAS 36. Swiss GAAP FER 10 always amortises intangibles - defaulting to 5 years when useful life is uncertain, up to a maximum of 20 years in justified cases - with no 'indefinite life' category.

title: Property, plant and equipment
lesson: IAS 16 lets an entity choose, by class of asset, between the cost model and the revaluation model for property, plant and equipment measured after initial recognition, and requires significant components with materially different useful lives (e.g. an aircraft engine vs its airframe) to be depreciated separately. Swiss GAAP FER 18 is more conservative and is generally built around the cost model only.
source: IAS 16 (cost vs revaluation model, component approach); Swiss GAAP FER 18

title: Impairment of assets
lesson: IAS 36 requires testing a cash-generating unit's recoverable amount (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use) against its carrying amount whenever there is an indicator of impairment - except goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles, which must be tested at least annually regardless of indicators (§12). Swiss GAAP FER 20 requires similar write-downs but with less prescriptive guidance on how to calculate the recoverable amount.

title: Financial instruments
lesson: IFRS 9 classifies financial assets based on the entity's business model and the instrument's contractual cash flow characteristics (the SPPI test), into amortised cost, FVOCI, or FVTPL categories, and requires an expected credit loss (ECL) impairment model that recognises losses before they're actually incurred. Swiss GAAP FER has no equivalent structured classification framework.

title: Provisions and contingencies
lesson: IAS 37 requires a provision to be recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow of resources is probable, and the amount can be reliably estimated - all three conditions must be met. If any condition fails (e.g. the outflow is only possible, not probable), it is instead a contingent liability, disclosed in the notes but not recognised as a liability.
source: IAS 37 (recognition criteria; provisions vs contingent liabilities)

title: Business combinations
lesson: IFRS 3 requires the acquisition method for all business combinations, recognising identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value and any goodwill as a residual, with no amortisation - only annual impairment testing. Swiss GAAP FER 30 gives more flexibility, allowing goodwill to be capitalised and amortised or offset directly against equity at acquisition, a choice IFRS 3 does not permit.
source: IFRS 3 (acquisition method, goodwill); Swiss GAAP FER 30

title: Consolidated financial statements
lesson: IFRS 10 defines control - the basis for consolidation - through power over the investee, exposure to variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns. This substance-based model can bring 'de facto control' situations into consolidation even with less than 50% of voting rights, if the remaining shares are widely dispersed.

title: Fair value measurement
lesson: IFRS 13 defines fair value as an exit price: the price that would be received to sell an asset, or paid to transfer a liability, in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date - not an entity-specific value or historical cost.

title: Income taxes
lesson: IAS 12 requires recognition of deferred tax assets and liabilities for temporary differences between an asset or liability's carrying amount and its tax base (e.g. different depreciation rates for accounting vs tax purposes), generally measured at the tax rates expected to apply when the difference reverses.

title: Auditing internal control over financial reporting
lesson: PCAOB AS 2201 governs the audit of internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) when integrated with the financial statement audit. The auditor's objective is to express an opinion on whether ICFR was effective in all material respects - if one or more material weaknesses exist, ICFR cannot be considered effective.

title: Audit risk assessment
lesson: ISA 315 (Revised 2019) requires the auditor to identify and assess the risks of material misstatement by understanding the entity and its environment, including its internal control, so that audit procedures can be designed to respond to those assessed risks (per ISA 330).

title: Presentation of financial statements (IFRS 18)
lesson: IFRS 18 (effective 1 January 2027, replacing IAS 1) requires every income and expense item in the statement of profit or loss to be classified into one of five categories - operating, investing, financing, income taxes, and discontinued operations - with two new mandatory subtotals: 'operating profit' and 'profit before financing and income taxes'. It also introduces mandatory disclosure of 'management-defined performance measures' (MPMs), reconciled to the nearest IFRS subtotal, bringing transparency to previously unregulated 'adjusted earnings' metrics.
source: IFRS 18 (issued April 2024, effective 1 Jan 2027, supersedes IAS 1)

title: Statement of cash flows
lesson: IAS 7 requires cash flows to be classified into operating, investing, and financing activities, and permits operating cash flows to be presented using either the direct method (gross receipts and payments) or the indirect method (profit adjusted for non-cash items and working capital movements) - IAS 7 encourages the direct method, but the indirect method dominates in practice.
source: IAS 7 (classification of cash flows, direct vs indirect method)

title: Events after the reporting period
lesson: IAS 10 distinguishes adjusting events (which provide further evidence of conditions that already existed at the reporting date, and require the financial statements to be adjusted) from non-adjusting events (which relate to conditions arising after the reporting date, and only require disclosure if material). Going concern is a special case: if management decides after year-end that it must liquidate, this is treated as an adjusting event so fundamental that the going concern basis itself is abandoned.
source: IAS 10 (adjusting vs non-adjusting events, going concern)

title: Government grants
lesson: IAS 20 requires a government grant to be recognised in profit or loss on a systematic basis over the periods in which the entity recognises the related expenses the grant is intended to compensate (§12) - for example, a grant funding a depreciable asset is recognised over that asset's useful life, matched against the depreciation charge. A grant that reimburses costs already incurred is instead recognised immediately as income.

title: Borrowing costs
lesson: IAS 23 requires borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction, or production of a 'qualifying asset' (one that necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for its intended use or sale) to be capitalised as part of that asset's cost, rather than expensed as incurred (§8). For funds borrowed specifically for the asset, the actual costs incurred are capitalised; for general borrowings, a weighted-average capitalisation rate is applied to the qualifying expenditure.

title: Earnings per share
lesson: IAS 33 requires basic EPS to be calculated as profit or loss attributable to ordinary equity holders of the parent, divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period - shares issued or bought back during the year are time-weighted by the number of days (or months) they were outstanding. Diluted EPS adjusts both the numerator and denominator for the effect of all dilutive potential ordinary shares (e.g. convertible instruments, share options under the treasury stock method).

title: Associates and the equity method
lesson: IAS 28 creates a rebuttable presumption of 'significant influence' - the power to participate in financial and operating policy decisions without control - whenever an investor holds 20% or more of an investee's voting power. An investee over which the investor has significant influence is an associate, accounted for using the equity method: the investment starts at cost and is then adjusted each period for the investor's share of the associate's post-acquisition profit or loss and OCI.

title: Employee benefits (pensions)
lesson: IAS 19 splits the change in a defined benefit pension's net liability/asset into two very differently-treated pieces: service cost and net interest go through profit or loss, while remeasurements (actuarial gains/losses, and the difference between actual and expected return on plan assets) go to other comprehensive income and are never recycled to profit or loss afterwards. Net interest is calculated by applying the discount rate used to measure the obligation to the net defined benefit liability or asset.
source: IAS 19 (service cost, net interest, remeasurements in OCI)

title: Foreign exchange translation
lesson: IAS 21 distinguishes an entity's functional currency (the currency of its primary economic environment - a factual determination) from its presentation currency (which it can choose freely). When translating a foreign operation into the group's presentation currency, assets and liabilities are translated at the closing rate, income and expenses at transaction-date (often average) rates, and the resulting exchange differences go to other comprehensive income and a separate translation reserve in equity - not to profit or loss.
source: IAS 21 (functional vs presentation currency, translation method)

title: Related party disclosures
lesson: IAS 24 requires disclosure of related party relationships, transactions, and outstanding balances (including commitments) whenever a related party relationship exists - control, joint control, significant influence, or key management personnel status - regardless of whether the transactions were priced on normal commercial (arm's length) terms. It also specifically requires disclosure of key management personnel compensation, by category.
source: IAS 24 (related party relationships, key management personnel compensation)

title: Share-based payment
lesson: IFRS 2 measures share-based payment transactions at the fair value of the equity instruments granted, determined at the grant date. For equity-settled arrangements (e.g. employee share options), that grant-date fair value is fixed and spread as an expense over the vesting period, with no remeasurement for later share price changes. For cash-settled arrangements, a liability is recognised and remeasured to fair value at every reporting date until settlement.
source: IFRS 2 (grant-date fair value; equity-settled vs cash-settled)

title: Operating segments
lesson: IFRS 8 requires an entity to identify its operating segments based on the internal reports reviewed by its chief operating decision maker (CODM - a function, not necessarily a single job title). A segment is 'reportable' if it meets any ONE of three 10% quantitative thresholds (revenue, profit or loss, or assets), and if the reportable segments' combined external revenue falls below 75% of total external revenue, further segments must be added until that threshold is met.

title: Joint arrangements
lesson: IFRS 11 splits joint arrangements into joint operations (where the parties have direct rights to the arrangement's assets and obligations for its liabilities, recognised as a direct share of assets/liabilities/revenues/expenses) and joint ventures (where the parties only have rights to the arrangement's net assets, accounted for using the equity method under IAS 28). Classification depends on the substance of the parties' rights and obligations, not merely on whether a separate legal vehicle is used.
source: IFRS 11 (joint operation vs joint venture classification)

title: Overall objectives of the auditor
lesson: ISA 200 establishes that the auditor's overall objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance - a high, but not absolute, level of assurance - that the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to report accordingly. Achieving this requires professional scepticism throughout the audit: a questioning mind that does not simply accept management's explanations at face value.

title: Audit documentation
lesson: ISA 230 requires documentation sufficient to enable an 'experienced auditor' with no prior connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing and extent of procedures performed, their results, and the significant matters and conclusions reached. A limited period after the report date is allowed to assemble the final file administratively, but no new audit procedures or conclusions may be added during that window.
source: ISA 230 (experienced auditor test, final file assembly)

title: Auditor's responsibilities relating to fraud
lesson: ISA 240 makes clear that the primary responsibility for preventing and detecting fraud rests with management and those charged with governance, not the auditor - but the auditor must still obtain reasonable assurance the financial statements are free from material misstatement due to fraud. Because the risk of management override of controls exists at every entity, ISA 240 mandates specific minimum procedures to address it (testing journal entries, reviewing estimates for bias, evaluating significant unusual transactions) regardless of the auditor's other risk assessments.
source: ISA 240 (management responsibility, mandatory procedures for override risk)

title: Communicating control deficiencies
lesson: ISA 265 requires the auditor to communicate control deficiencies identified during the audit. 'Significant deficiencies' - important enough to merit the attention of those charged with governance - must be communicated in writing and on a timely basis; less important deficiencies, which still merit management's attention, can be communicated orally to an appropriate level of management.
source: ISA 265 (significant deficiencies, written vs oral communication)

title: Materiality in planning and performing an audit
lesson: ISA 320 requires the auditor to set overall materiality for the financial statements as a whole, and then also set 'performance materiality' - a lower amount applied to individual transactions, balances or disclosures - specifically to reduce the risk that the total of small, undetected or uncorrected misstatements could aggregate to something material. Materiality is not fixed at planning; it must be revised if new information emerges that would have led to a different judgement at the outset.

title: Audit evidence
lesson: ISA 500 requires the auditor to obtain 'sufficient appropriate' audit evidence to draw reasonable conclusions: sufficiency measures quantity, appropriateness measures quality (relevance and reliability). The two are interrelated - higher-quality (e.g. external, independently obtained) evidence can reduce the quantity needed, while higher assessed risk increases the quantity required.

title: Audit evidence for specific items
lesson: ISA 501 sets out specific evidence requirements for three areas prone to misstatement or management bias: inventory (attendance at the physical count, or alternative procedures if attendance is impracticable), litigation and claims (enquiry of management and, typically, direct communication with external legal counsel), and segment information (understanding how segments are determined and testing disclosure compliance).
source: ISA 501 (inventory, litigation and claims, segment information)

title: Analytical procedures
lesson: ISA 520 allows analytical procedures - comparing recorded amounts to an auditor-developed expectation - to be used as a substantive procedure. Reliance depends on the plausibility of the relationship being tested, the reliability of the underlying data, and the auditor's industry knowledge. Any significant unexplained fluctuation must be investigated through management enquiry and corroboration, or further procedures.
source: ISA 520 (analytical procedures as substantive evidence, investigating fluctuations)

title: Audit sampling
lesson: ISA 530 governs the design, selection and evaluation of audit samples when testing less than 100% of a population. Having found exceptions in a sample, the auditor must project the misstatement rate to the population as a whole (not just report the raw exceptions found) and assess whether that projected result indicates a risk of material misstatement.

title: Auditing accounting estimates
lesson: ISA 540 treats accounting estimates (depreciation, provisions, expected credit losses, fair values) as inherently higher-risk because they involve subjective management judgement and carry a risk of bias. Recognised audit approaches include testing the process and assumptions management used to develop the estimate, and/or developing an independent point estimate or range for comparison.
source: ISA 540 (subjectivity, testing management's process, independent estimate)

title: Auditing related party relationships and transactions
lesson: ISA 550 builds on the related party definitions in IAS 24 to guide the auditor's procedures for identifying related party relationships and transactions, and evaluating whether they have been properly accounted for and disclosed. Related party transactions - especially those not on normal market terms - carry heightened fraud and management override risk, since they can be used to move value out of the entity or manipulate reported results.
source: ISA 550 (related party audit procedures, fraud risk)

title: Subsequent events (audit perspective)
lesson: ISA 560 requires the auditor to obtain evidence that events between the reporting date and the date of the auditor's report requiring adjustment or disclosure (per IAS 10) have been properly reflected, and sets out specific procedures for facts discovered after the report is signed but before the financial statements are issued - which can require re-opening the audit, amending the financial statements, and issuing a new report.
source: ISA 560 (subsequent events, facts discovered after the report date)

title: Going concern (audit perspective)
lesson: Under ISA 570, assessing the appropriateness of the going concern basis is management's responsibility; the auditor evaluates that assessment and the related evidence. If a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is not modified for that reason alone, but the auditor's report must include a dedicated section drawing attention to the disclosure - inadequate disclosure, by contrast, does lead to a modified opinion.

title: Forming and reporting the audit opinion
lesson: ISA 700 governs the unmodified opinion - concluding the financial statements are fairly presented, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable framework. ISA 705 governs modifications (qualified, adverse, or disclaimer of opinion) when a material misstatement exists or sufficient appropriate evidence cannot be obtained. ISA 706's Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter paragraphs highlight something already properly presented or disclosed - they must never be used as a substitute for a modification that ISA 705 actually requires.

title: Quality management for audit firms
lesson: ISQM 1 (effective from December 2022, replacing ISQC 1) requires firms performing audits, reviews, or other assurance engagements to design, implement and operate a risk-based system of quality management, tailored to the firm's own nature and circumstances - identifying quality risks, assessing them, and designing responses, rather than following a generic, one-size-fits-all checklist.
